parts:
I am hoping someone can give me some guidance on how to use simmer to model the following situation:

Ships arriving randomly to a dock where the product is loaded into a refinery tank. The loaded product is then consumed at the refinery at a given rate.  The refinery tank has finite inventory (non-zero queue).  The complication arises that if the refinery tank is full, product should not be loaded in the dock until inventory space becomes available.  I have tried to use set attribute and conditional logic to identify the situation when the tank is full to prevent the ship from being loaded into the refinery tank.  The dock resource will have infinite queue as I am trying to determine the optimum refinery tank capacity to minimize wait time. However, with my logic the arrival is being rejected.  Any suggestions on how to model this scenario with simmer would be appreciated.

 

My code is provided below.


Thanks,

Jose

library(ggplot2)

library(plyr)

library(dplyr)

library(parallel)

library(doBy)

library(xlsx)

 

 

set.seed(1234)

lambda3 <- 0.001  #average one 500 Mbbl ship every 8 days or 100Mbbls per day

lambda4 <- 0.001  #average one 500 Mbbl ship every 7 days  or

lambda4 <- 0.001  #NA

    t1<-create_trajectory() %>%

 

    set_attribute("available1", function() {

     if (env %>%  get_queue_count("Term2")<2) 1

   # timeout(function() 26.5/24) %>%

Hi Jose, welcome to the list.

I don't know if I understand the problem. I cannot identify which parts of your model correspond to which elements of the problem description. What are the "terms"? Why does one of them have an infinite queue while the others have finite ones (that's why you have rejections, by the way)? What's the meaning of each trajectory?

What I understand from your description is that you have a producer-consumer problem. This can be modelled more naturally with a resource like a container or a storage supporting put/get methods. This kind of resources are not implemented in simmer yet, but they're in our schedule. Meanwhile, since simmer's resource is pretty flexible, you can mimic the put/get behaviour thanks to the independence of seize/release.

Therefore, from your description, I would expect one trajectory per producer, which only seizes (puts stuff into) the resource, and one trajectory per consumer, which only releases (gets stuff from) the resource. However, all your trajectories perform seizes and releases, which seems confusing to me.

Also I would suggest you refine your optimisation objective. Because if you only want to minimise the waiting time, the response is immediate: an infinite capacity minimises the waiting time. So I suspect that you have more restrictions to apply.

Regards,
Iñaki

So you don't need attributes at all, and all your resources must have infinite queues:
  • A ship tries to seize the dock (a seize blocks while the arrival stays in the queue).
  • When the ship gains the dock, it tries to seize the corresponding tank. So if the resource's server (the tank) is full, it waits in the resource's infinite queue (waits in the dock). 
  • When the latter seize unblocks, it means that the cargo is finally in the tank, so the ship leaves.
And of course, you'll need another trajectory for releasing the tanks.

So you don't need attributes at all, and all your resources must have infinite queues:
  • A ship tries to seize the dock (a seize blocks while the arrival stays in the queue).
